newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish zloty devaluation rate cut seen in H2 1997.
newsitem.headline: Polish zloty devaluation rate cut seen in H2 1997.

text.p: The National Bank of Poland may cut the zloty's devaluation rate in the second half of this year when inflation slows, analysts said.

The budget envisages that the zloty will be devalued by nine percent in 1997 through the monthly devaluation rate, also known as the crawling-peg mechanism, but analysts said the target would not be met.
The devaluation rate is currently one percent a month against a basket of currencies.

"The central bank will likely try to take markets by surprise with a move in the crawling-peg, which can be expected no earlier than in mid-year," said Jan Mieczkowski, treasurer of Deutsche Bank Polska SA.
The independent National Bank of Poland, which controls the zloty exchange rate, has said that the nine percent devaluation was only a target and that it may not be met in 1997.
Analysts said the NBP was unlikely to slow down the zloty's devaluation until after inflation, at 18.5 percent year-on-year in December, fell well below 18 percent.

"When inflation falls below 18 percent and remains there, the central bank may consider a slower zloty devaluation rate -- perhaps between May and July," said Andrzej Ladko, chief dealer at Bank Handlowy SA.
Analysts said that although a slower crawling peg would help curb inflation by cutting import prices, it would also hurt exporters, who have a strong lobby for a weaker zloty.
"It is a very political matter, but if the devaluation rate is not cut along with falling inflation, it could discourage foreign (direct) investment," Handlowy's Ladko said.
Some analysts said a crawling peg cut could come as late as the fourth quarter of 1997, after parliamentary polls due in September.

"After its currency-buying interventions a few weeks back, the NBP seems intent to keep the zloty from firming...it may hold the rate flat until the last quarter of the year," said Wlodzimierz Osak, chief dealer at Pekao SA.

Analysts said the zloty, which was devaluated by an 13.26 percent against a basket of five western currencies in 1996, still gained in real-terms for many exporters, as producer prices increased by only 10.5 percent last year.

However, exports grew sluggishly last year as a cool economic climate in Germany and other EU countries, the destination of nearly 70 percent of Poland's exports, severely limited demand for Polish products.

In the January-November period of 1996 registered exports grew 5.2 percent while imports boomed by 31.3 percent, widening the trade deficit to $7.2 billion from $1.3 billion in the same period of 1995.
